Paper_name: The oscillatory fingerprints of self-prioritization: Novel markers in spectral EEG for self-relevant processing
Summary: This EEG study investigated the spectral dynamics of self-prioritization using a familiarity-confound free matching task. Participants associated arbitrary shapes with 'self' or 'stranger', and behavioral results showed self-prioritization effects in reaction time and accuracy. EEG analysis revealed two significant self-prioritization effects in spectral power: one in the delta/theta band (2–7 Hz) and one in the beta band (19–29 Hz). Drift-diffusion modeling linked beta activity to evidence accumulation and delta/theta activity to response selection. The findings suggest these oscillatory patterns serve as novel biomarkers for self-relevant processing.
Author: Céline C. Haciahmet, Marius Golubickis, Sarah Schäfer, Christian Frings, Bernhard Pastötter
Conclusion: The study identified two novel oscillatory biomarkers of self-prioritization: decreased beta suppression associated with more efficient sensorimotor processing of self-associated features, and increased delta/theta power linked to facilitated retrieval of self-relevant information across a distributed associative network. These spectral EEG markers indicate that self-prioritization functions as an 'associative glue' for the self-concept, with distinct frequency bands supporting different cognitive processes (evidence accumulation vs. response selection).
